text: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 (D&C Act) and Rules 1945 regulate the import, manufacture, distribution, and sale of drugs and cosmetics in India. For AYUSH sector, key relevance: Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani (ASU) drugs are regulated under Chapter IVA and Schedule E. Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) is the regulatory authority. State Drug Controllers handle state-level licensing. Key purposes: ensure drug quality, safety, and efficacy; prevent adulteration and misbranding; regulate advertising claims. Non-compliance leads to penalties including imprisonment and fines.

Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani drugs fall into two categories under D&C Act: 1) Classical/Authorized drugs (Schedule E) — formulations mentioned in authoritative texts (Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Bhavaprakash, etc.), can be manufactured without separate approval, follow standardized processes. 2) Patent/Proprietary medicines — new formulations developed by manufacturers, require specific approval and clinical evidence. For AYUSH startups: if your formulation is based on a classical reference, manufacturing license is simpler. If it's a new proprietary formulation, additional approvals and stability studies required.

To manufacture ASU drugs in India, obtain: 1) Manufacturing license from State Drug Controller under Rule 158-B. Requirements: qualified technical staff (degree/diploma in Ayurveda/Siddha/Unani), GMP-compliant premises, quality control lab, approved formulations. 2) For export: additional WHO-GMP certification recommended. Application process: submit Form 25D with fee, plant inspection by drug inspector, license issued if compliant (Form 26D). License valid for 5 years, renewable. For proprietary medicines, additionally submit: Form 33/44, stability data, safety data, and efficacy evidence.

GMP requirements for ASU drugs under Schedule T of D&C Rules: Factory premises: adequate space, ventilation, lighting, and hygiene. Equipment: suitable for manufacturing, properly maintained and calibrated. Personnel: trained staff, qualified technical supervisor, no communicable diseases. Raw materials: authenticated botanical/mineral/animal materials, supplier qualification, testing on receipt. Manufacturing: batch records, in-process controls, documentation. Quality control: testing of finished products, stability studies, retention samples. Packaging and labeling: correct labels, batch numbers, expiry dates, proper storage. Self-inspection: regular internal audits.

Critical distinction under D&C Act: DRUGS (Chapter IV/IVA) — articles intended for diagnosis, cure, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of disease. Regulated more strictly. COSMETICS (Chapter III) — articles rubbed, poured, sprinkled, or sprayed on the body for cleansing, beautifying, or altering appearance. Less strict regulation. Classification determines which rules apply. For AYUSH products: if product claims to treat acne (disease), it's a drug. If it claims to 'cleanse' or 'beautify' skin without therapeutic claims, it may be a cosmetic. Wrong classification leads to legal issues. When in doubt, consult CDSCO or apply for clarification.

ASU drug labeling under Rule 161: Name of drug (generic and brand), List of ingredients with quantities, Net content, Name and address of manufacturer, License number, Batch/lot number, Date of manufacture, Expiry date ('use before'), Directions for use, Warnings (if applicable), Maximum retail price (MRP), 'For external use only' if applicable, Storage instructions. For classical preparations: reference to authoritative text. For proprietary medicines: composition formula approved by licensing authority. False or misleading labeling is an offense under Section 17/18.

Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954 restricts AYUSH drug advertising. Prohibited claims: claiming to cure diseases in Schedule J (cancer, diabetes, heart disease, etc.), claiming magical/miraculous effects, using government/medical body endorsements without permission. Allowed: truthful claims supported by evidence, statements from authoritative Ayurvedic texts for classical preparations. Penalties: first offense — up to 6 months imprisonment and/or Rs 5,000 fine; subsequent offense — up to 1 year and/or Rs 10,000. For AYUSH marketers: avoid disease cure claims; use 'supports wellness', 'traditional remedy for' language; maintain evidence files for all claims.

Importing ASU drugs into India requires: 1) Import license from CDSCO (under Form 8 for manufacturer, Form 10 for trader). 2) No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the overseas manufacturer. 3) Compliance with Indian quality standards. 4) Labeling in English and regional language. 5) Certificate of analysis. Registration not required for ASU drugs (unlike allopathic), but CDSCO can demand registration for certain categories. For AYUSH exporters: target countries may have their own requirements (FDA registration for USA, EFSA notification for EU). India has mutual recognition agreements with few countries — check target market regulations before export.

ASU drug quality testing follows: 1) Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) — official compendium of quality standards for Ayurvedic drugs, published by Ministry of AYUSH. 2) Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) — for ingredients also used in modern medicine. 3) In-house specifications — for proprietary formulations, must be approved by licensing authority. Tests include: identity (correct herb/ingredient), purity (absence of adulterants, heavy metals within limits), potency (active constituent levels), microbial limits, stability. Government/empaneled labs: Central Drug Testing Laboratory (CDTL), Regional Drug Testing Labs, AYUSH-approved testing labs.

Penalties for violations of D&C Act: Manufacturing without license (Section 18) — imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 5,000; repeat offense up to 5 years. Sale of adulterated drugs (Section 27) — imprisonment up to 3 years and fine; if causing grievous hurt up to 5 years. Sale of spurious drugs (Section 27A) — imprisonment 10 years to life and fine. Misbranding (Section 27) — imprisonment up to 1 year and fine. Drug inspectors can: enter and inspect premises, collect samples, seize suspected drugs, initiate prosecution. For AYUSH businesses: maintain compliance, keep records, cooperate with inspectors, consult legal counsel if notices received.

Exporting AYUSH products: 1) Domestic: manufacturing license + sale license sufficient. 2) Export: additionally may need Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CoPP) from CDSCO, WHO-GMP certification, export license from DGFT (for controlled substances). Market-specific: USA requires FDA registration and compliance (DSHEA for supplements, NDA for drugs). EU requires Novel Food approval for non-traditional ingredients. Middle East requires SFDA/GCC registration. Australia requires TGA listing. India-specific advantages: government provides export incentives (MEIS/RoDTEP), AYUSH export promotion through PHARMEXCIL. Documents: quality certificate, free sale certificate, phytosanitary certificate (for plant-based).
